name: Carla Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is lectures on mechatronics, which is a mix of mechanics, electronics and code, and then long afternoons in the workshop soldering things that mostly don't work yet. I live in a flat with three people near the canal, and I work Saturdays packing orders at a warehouse by the ring road. My parents cover roughly half my costs and my wage covers the rest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What drew you to mechatronics and robotics?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I built a line-following robot with my uncle when I was twelve and it drove straight into a wall, and I was hooked. My mum is a physio and my dad is a school caretaker, so nobody in the family designs machines. My results were average, so I'm not a star student, but I'm curious and I'll try anything. I use AI tools every day, for debugging code, for checking my maths and for planning my weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's another tool, and the real work is still building things. My friends would agree, and some would be a bit relieved. Online I'd post about a robot arm project I'm building, because that's more fun than arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good, since mechatronics doesn't depend on a hype cycle. The warehouse job might change a bit, but robots there are already part of life. I'd still have the normal worries about money, the flat and paying back the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, finish the first year, and look for a summer placement at a company that builds automation. I'd keep working at the warehouse, because I learn from watching the robots there. I'd also enter the university robotics competition with my flatmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Calm, even happy. It's what I hoped the world would be like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still be on your mind in that quiet version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan, mostly, and whether placements will be paid. My parents help but they can't pay everything. If the warehouse cut my Saturdays, I'd have to find another job fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the warehouse cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask around the robotics lab for a paid assistant job, or offer to repair friends' drones and e-bikes. I like making things, so I'd rather earn money that way than stacking shelves.

say: I'd say it's another **tool** and the real work is still building things.
Online I'd post about my robot arm project instead of arguing.
think: Mechatronics doesn't depend on a **hype cycle**, so I feel good about my degree.
I still worry about the loan and the flat.
do: Finish first year, look for a summer **placement** at an automation firm, and enter the robotics competition.
Keep the warehouse job and learn from the robots there.
feel: I feel **calm**, even happy, since this is the world I hoped for.
S0.quote: I like making things, so I'd rather earn money that way than stacking shelves.
fieldNote: Genuinely **calm**: her field is hands-on and she uses AI daily, so a plateau costs her nothing.
Money is the only worry, and she has a creative fallback.
Learns from the warehouse robots on her Saturday job.

steps.text: Apply for a summer placement at an automation company
Enter the university robotics competition with her flatmates
Repair friends' drones and e-bikes for pocket money if hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: the thinking tasks go first and machines come later. I'd tell my friends in coding to branch out, and I'd tell the warehouse supervisor that his planning jobs are the ones at risk. Online I'd share a couple of demos showing what AI can and can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my field is lucky because it sits between thinking and hands-on. AI helps me design and debug, but someone still has to build and fix real machines. The risk is that fewer junior roles exist, so I'd need to stand out with projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more deliberately, like for simulations and for checking designs. I'd build a portfolio of working robots, film them and post them. And I'd try to get on a placement where I can work with both software and hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but curious. I'd like to see what happens, even if it keeps me up sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the people who aren't as ready as you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help my flatmate Noor, who's doing the same course but never touches AI. I'd show her one thing per week, like how to use it to check a circuit. It's easier to learn from a friend than from a lecture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the placements dry up. Companies might hire fewer juniors and go for experienced people. I'd start applying a year earlier than everyone else, just to get ahead of the rush.

Online I'd share demos of what AI can and can't do.
think: My field sits between thinking and **hands-on** work, so I'm lucky.
The risk is fewer junior roles, so I need projects to stand out.
do: Use AI for **simulations** and design checks, and build a portfolio of working robots.
Apply for placements a year earlier than everyone else.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but curious, wanting to see what happens.
S1.quote: Companies might hire fewer juniors and go for experienced people.
fieldNote: Her **curiosity** keeps her uneasy rather than anxious.
Tests herself against the junior-role squeeze and acts early.
Helps a flatmate, Noor, learn AI one step per week.

steps.text: Film and post working robot builds as a portfolio
Use AI for simulations and checking designs
Apply for placements a year earlier than classmates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to get this right, fast. I'd call for governments to get companies to share what they know, and I'd talk about it with my lecturers. At the warehouse I'd say what I see: the robots are already close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think it's the biggest thing that'll happen in my life. My degree is half thinking work, which goes first, but the hands-on half lasts until about 2031. I'm in a better spot than most but not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the robotics and hands-on side. I'd try to get hired part-time by the university lab, since the people building the robots will matter longest. I'd also keep my spending low and save every pound, because everything is about to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a little thrilled, which is a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years' warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It cuts out the slow plan. I'd stop thinking about my degree as a ladder and think of it as a toolbox. I'd pick the modules that give me real skills and skip the ones that only give grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum, the physio, that her job is safe for a long time because it's hands-on, but I'd say it carefully. I'd tell my dad the school will keep him on. And I'd say don't worry about me, I'm already moving.

say: I'd say we need to get this right, **fast**, and companies should share what they know.
At the warehouse I'd say the robots are already close.
think: It's the biggest thing that'll happen in my life, and my degree is half **thinking work**.
The hands-on half lasts until about 2031, so I'm better placed but not safe.
do: Go all in on **robotics**, and try to get hired part-time by the university lab.
Keep spending low and save every pound.
feel: I feel **anxious** and a little thrilled, a strange mix.
S2.quote: I'd stop thinking about my degree as a ladder and think of it as a toolbox.
fieldNote: Reframes the degree as a **toolbox**, choosing modules for skills over grades.
Anxious and thrilled together; she moves fast without panic.
Tells her parents their hands-on jobs are safe for longer, carefully.

steps.text: Ask the university robotics lab for a part-time assistant job
Choose modules that give real hardware skills over easy grades
Save every spare pound from the warehouse wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty to act if people act now. I'd tell friends to learn how these systems work, not just use them. I'd say governments should fund retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate in 2029, so I'd arrive just as the thinking AI takes over. That's a risk. But I'd have built robots, used the tools for years and made contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take placements every summer, join a robotics start-up if I could, and learn a second skill like electrical installation. I'd keep working weekends and put a bit in savings. I'd also keep making things on my own time, because they build the best portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, steady. A deadline gives me something to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's room for a proper plan. With two years I'd throw out the degree and rush, while with five I can finish it and add things. I'd also try to build something that sells, like a small robot kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which people around you would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Noor, who's in the same course but hates change. I'd give her the push she needs, and I'd show her I'm doing the same. People need to see someone else move first.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty** if people act now, and governments should fund retraining.
I'd tell friends to learn how these systems work, not just use them.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 just as thinking AI takes over, which is a **risk**.
By then I'd have built robots and made contacts.
do: Take a **placement** every summer and learn a second skill like electrical installation.
Build a small robot kit to sell.
feel: I feel **steady**, since a deadline gives me something to aim at.
S3.quote: With two years I'd throw out the degree and rush, while with five I can finish it and add things.
fieldNote: Five years gives her room to **stack** skills; she'd even try selling a robot kit.
Concern for Noor shows she leads by example.
Unease stays because 2029 graduation lands just as thinking AI matures.

steps.text: Take a summer placement every year in robotics or automation
Learn electrical installation as a second skill
Design a small robot kit to sell online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and we have time to get it right. I'd tell people to build things, to try tools, and to look after each other. I'd tell politicians to start the education changes now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 28, maybe running a small robotics company or leading a team. The thinking AI would be my colleague, and robots would be the product. I'd hope my family is doing fine too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at an automation firm for a few years, and then try my own thing. I'd save for a deposit and keep learning. I'd also stay in touch with my university lab for contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Happy, honestly. I'd sleep very well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still go wrong in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The timing could be off, and I'd be caught short if the ten years turned into five. I'd keep spare money in case and not take too much risk with a loan. It's not a big thing, just common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently starting this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop worrying about being an average student. Nobody will ask for my first-year marks when I show them a robot that works. I'd say yes to more projects and less to extra shifts.

say: I'd say it's **exciting** and we have time to get it right.
I'd tell politicians to start the education changes now.
think: By 2036 I could be running a small **robotics** company or leading a team.
I'd hope my family is doing fine too.
do: Finish the degree, work at an **automation** firm, then try my own thing.
Save for a deposit and stay in touch with the university lab.
feel: I feel **happy**, and I'd sleep very well.
S4.quote: Nobody will ask for my first-year marks when I show them a robot that works.
fieldNote: Plain **calm**: ten years suits her curious, adaptive style.
Keeps a small cushion in case the timing is wrong.
Average marks bother her more than the AI.

steps.text: Join an automation firm after the degree for a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, though I'd cope better than most. The speed is what bothers me, because families and schools can't change in time. What would help is early retraining, paid placements and companies that keep on young engineers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as fearless as I sound. I like new things, but I worry about my parents. If I can bring them along, I think I'd feel fine about almost any of these.

headlineQuote: I'm not as fearless as I sound. I like new things, but I worry about my parents.
portrait: Carla is an **18-year-old** mechatronics student who packs orders at a warehouse on Saturdays and uses AI tools every day.
She sits in the political centre, learns by building things and moves **early** on new technology.
Her field is half thinking work and half hands-on, so she feels better placed than most.
She is **calm** when change is slow, and anxious but thrilled when it is fast.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because families and schools can't change fast enough.
whatWouldHelp: Early **retraining**, paid placements and companies that keep hiring young engineers.
